story_text.value:
I built my own workout app for my smart trainer (a Tacx Neo 2t). Added a system of streaks and points to motivate me train and it has become part of my daily routine. I am curious to know if it could be useful to someone else?

I just wanted a quick way to train when I had some spare minutes. I didn’t want to subscribe to a full blown game. You pick how long you want to ride (any custom length or predefined workouts), connect your trainer from the browser via bluetooth, and it sets the resistance for you via ERG to give you a complete workout with wam-up, intervals and cool-down. No downloads, no account and no cookies. Everything stays in your browser and is designed to get your pedaling as soon as possible.

It needs a browser that supports Web bluetooth (like Chrome or Edge on a computer) and a bluetooth smart trainers that supports FTMS (should be most). I have only tested it with my Tacx Neo 2t, so I’d love to hear how it works for other people. Thanks!

title.value: Show HN: A browser app that controls my bike trainer over Bluetooth

story_text.value:
You might have seen PhotoCraft, an open-source Photoshop-style editor. It's great, but it was missing one important ingredient: generative AI. LayerShop fills that gap, and unlike Photoshop, it can run the models locally on your own GPU, for free.

Here are the AI features you get with LayerShop:

- a guided ComfyUI install (the engine)

- guided download and setup of local models, including the latest ones like MOSS Image, Ming, Ernie, FLUX.3 Klein, Z-Image, Krea 2 and Ideogram 4

- support for the latest cloud (paid) models like GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst and Flare, FLUX 3, Grok Imagine 2 and Nano Banana Pro

It supports text to image, image to image, inpainting and outpainting, named image references, targeted or whole-image edits, style transfer, photo restoration, relighting and more.

All of that in a familiar Photoshop-style UI, on layers with transparency, blend modes and masks.

Every generated layer remembers which model, prompt and settings made it. You can still tweak the advanced settings if you like: number of steps, seed, CFG scale, LoRA strength and more.

It's a first preview: Windows only, NVIDIA for local models, and not code-signed yet. 3-minute demo: https://youtu.be/dCBiipZ03dA

title.value: Show HN: LayerShop – a love child of ComfyUI and PhotoCraft

story_text.value:
I built Seqora as a solo developer because I was tired of DBeaver and TablePlus, the tools I was using. None of them felt like modern tooling. DBeaver is mature, but it lacks customization and it’s slow. TablePlus puts too many limits on its free tier, like only allowing two tabs open at a time. What I wanted to do differently in Seqora was to let me visualize different objects, like indexes, partitions, etc. Another thing I found most tools lacked was a way to figure out what’s slowing down a complex query, so I built a visual EXPLAIN that shows where the time goes. I put the main focus on those two.

The next thing was being able to work on a connection visually using diagrams, so I can see how things are connected and make changes by drag and drop. Once everything is done, I can review all the SQL that will run.

I made sure the things you need for a daily driver are free, so there’s no limit on the number of queries, connections or tabs. The deep-dive parts, the object views, visual EXPLAIN and schema diagrams, are in Pro. Pro is currently $5.99/month or $49/year. It’s pre-1.0, currently at 0.4.6. It supports macOS (Apple Silicon) and Windows, and Linux is coming soon.

It’s built with Tauri, Rust and Svelte. Most of the code was written with Claude Code and ChatGPT. I made the decisions and did the reviewing and testing.

I’d love it if you tried it and told me what you don’t like so I can improve it, and also what you hate about your current workbench.

title.value: Show HN: Seqora – Desktop DB Workbench for PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite

story_text.value:
Hey y’all! I’m a product designer (with adhd, this will come back) currently working on learning engineering to get on the design engineering bandwagon. Doing research on safari, chrome and llms felt horribly decentralized due to the lack of visual and contextual history, as my method of research is to get deep into granular information in order to understand new concepts in depth.

This made me so fed up that I wanted a way to create a Time Machine through my research in order to track the context of why I ended up where I was and be able to return to sources that interested me. I call it NODE Research Browser.

I baked in a few features; 1. Research Trails - An .MD record of a research session you can jump in and out of, export and share. 2. Multi-browser views of up to four at the same time to compare data. I also had to implement media auto play because I love ambient sound in the background. You can have more than 4 tabs open but double pinching will let you select which four tabs are in view. 3. Auto crawls to the next page across niche sites using key words present in the site in view, this auto refreshes. 4. LLM integration via MCP and API calls to ask questions on a topic, browse via agents and see their trail. 5. It’s completely free because I don’t know how to monetize it yet.

Let me know what you think, I can send a 4 minute survey that will really help me.

title.value: Show HN: Node research browser for knowledge networking
